prompt: In a Helm 3 chart directory, which file holds the chart's name, `version`, `appVersion`, and dependency declarations?
options: `Chart.yaml`
`values.yaml`
`templates/_helpers.tpl`
`Chart.lock`
optionNotes: `Chart.yaml` is the chart's metadata file: `apiVersion`, `name`, `version`, `appVersion`, `description`, and `dependencies` all live here, so it is correct.
`values.yaml` holds the default configuration values that templates read via `.Values`; it says nothing about the chart's own version or dependencies.
`_helpers.tpl` is a partials file for named templates (`define`) that other templates `include`; it renders no Kubernetes objects and carries no metadata.
`Chart.lock` is generated by `helm dependency update` to pin the exact resolved dependency versions; you declare dependencies in `Chart.yaml`, not here.
explanation: `Chart.yaml` is mandatory and describes the chart itself. In Helm 3 (`apiVersion: v2`) it also carries the `dependencies:` list that used to live in a separate `requirements.yaml` in Helm 2. `helm dependency update` reads those entries and writes the resolved versions to `Chart.lock`.
example:
apiVersion: v2
name: web
description: Frontend service
type: application
version: 1.4.0        # chart version (SemVer 2)
appVersion: "2.9.1"   # version of the app being packaged
dependencies:
  - name: redis
    version: "~19.0.0"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
diagram:
flowchart TD
    C["web chart directory"] --> Y["Chart.yaml metadata and dependencies"]
    C --> V["values.yaml defaults"]
    C --> T["templates/ manifests and _helpers.tpl"]
    C --> S["charts/ vendored subcharts"]
    Y -->|"helm dependency update"| L["Chart.lock pinned versions"]

prompt: Which `helm` command renders a chart's templates locally to stdout without contacting the Kubernetes API server?
options: `helm template`
`helm install --dry-run`
`helm show all`
`helm get manifest`
optionNotes: `helm template` renders the templates entirely client-side and prints the resulting YAML; it needs no cluster connection, so it is correct.
`helm install --dry-run` also renders manifests but, unless you add `--dry-run=client`, it still talks to the API server (for example to validate resources and evaluate `lookup`).
`helm show all` prints the chart's `Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, README and CRDs as stored in the package; it does not render templates.
`helm get manifest` fetches the rendered manifest of an already-installed release from the cluster's release Secret, so it needs a live release.
explanation: `helm template` is the standard way to inspect rendered output in CI or feed it into `kubectl apply`, GitOps tools, or policy scanners. Because it is fully offline, `.Capabilities` defaults to a built-in Kubernetes version (override with `--kube-version` and `--api-versions`) and `lookup` returns an empty result. Use `helm install --dry-run=server` when you need server-side information.
example:
$ helm template web ./web -f values-prod.yaml --kube-version 1.31.0 > rendered.yaml
$ kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered.yaml
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["chart plus values"] -->|"helm template"| R["rendered YAML on stdout"]
    R --> CI["lint, policy scan, GitOps commit"]
    C -->|"helm install --dry-run=server"| K["API server validation and lookup"]

prompt: Where does Helm 3 store the metadata for each release revision by default?
options: In a Kubernetes `Secret` in the release's namespace
In a `ConfigMap` in the `kube-system` namespace
In the Tiller pod's local database
In `~/.helm/releases` on the client machine
optionNotes: Helm 3 writes one `Secret` of type `helm.sh/release.v1` per revision, named `sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<revision>`, in the release namespace; this is correct.
ConfigMap storage in `kube-system` was Helm 2's Tiller default. Helm 3 can use ConfigMaps only when you explicitly set `HELM_DRIVER=configmap`.
Tiller was removed in Helm 3; there is no server-side component at all.
Helm 3 keeps cache and config on the client (`$HELM_CACHE_HOME`, `$HELM_CONFIG_HOME`) but release state lives in the cluster so any operator sees the same history.
explanation: Helm 3 has no Tiller, so release state is stored in the cluster next to the workload. Each revision is a gzipped, base64-encoded `Secret` containing the chart, values, and rendered manifest. This is why `helm history` works from any machine and why RBAC on Secrets in the namespace governs who can see or roll back a release. The storage driver can be switched via `HELM_DRIVER` (`secret`, `configmap`, `memory`, `sql`).
example:
$ kubectl get secret -n shop -l owner=helm
NAME                            TYPE                 DATA   AGE
sh.helm.release.v1.web.v1       helm.sh/release.v1   1      9d
sh.helm.release.v1.web.v2       helm.sh/release.v1   1      2d
diagram:
flowchart LR
    H["helm upgrade web"] --> S2["Secret sh.helm.release.v1.web.v2"]
    S1["Secret v1 superseded"] -.-> S2
    S2 -->|"helm history and rollback read"| H2["helm CLI on any machine"]
    S2 --> NS["namespace shop"]

prompt: You run `helm upgrade web ./web --set image.tag=2.0` and then later `helm upgrade web ./web --set replicas=5`. After the second upgrade, what is `image.tag` in the live release?
options: It reverts to the chart's default because `--set image.tag=2.0` was not repeated
It stays `2.0` because Helm always merges with previous values
The second upgrade fails because `image.tag` is missing
It becomes an empty string
optionNotes: Correct. By default `helm upgrade` starts from the chart's `values.yaml` plus only the values given on this command; previous overrides are discarded unless you pass `--reuse-values` or repeat them.

Merging with the previous release's values happens only with `--reuse-values` (or `--reset-then-reuse-values`); it is not the default, and mixing it with a new chart version can silently pin stale defaults.
Missing values do not fail an upgrade unless a template uses `required` on that key; here the default from `values.yaml` is used.
Helm never blanks values; it either uses the chart default or the supplied override.
explanation: This is one of the most common Helm surprises. Each `helm upgrade` computes values from scratch: chart defaults, then `-f` files, then `--set`. Overrides from earlier revisions are not carried forward unless you use `--reuse-values`. The safest practice is to keep all overrides in a versioned values file and always pass it, so every upgrade is reproducible.
example:
$ helm upgrade web ./web -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=2.0   # revision 2
$ helm upgrade web ./web -f values-prod.yaml --set replicas=5      # revision 3: image.tag back to default!
$ helm get values web   # shows only what was passed to the last upgrade
diagram:
flowchart LR
    D["values.yaml defaults"] --> M["merge"]
    F["-f files in order"] --> M
    S["--set flags"] --> M
    P["previous release values"] -.->|"only with --reuse-values"| M
    M --> R["values for this revision"]

prompt: What does the `--atomic` flag do on `helm install` or `helm upgrade`?
options: Waits for resources to become ready and rolls back (or deletes on install) automatically if the operation fails
Applies all manifests in a single Kubernetes transaction so partial updates are impossible
Locks the release so no other client can upgrade it concurrently
Skips hooks so the release is applied in one pass
optionNotes: Correct. `--atomic` implies `--wait`; if readiness is not reached within `--timeout`, an upgrade is rolled back to the previous revision and a fresh install is uninstalled.
Kubernetes has no multi-object transactions; Helm still applies objects one by one. `--atomic` is about cleanup after failure, not atomic application.
Helm 3 does serialise operations on the same release via the pending state, but that is independent of `--atomic`.
Hooks still run with `--atomic`; `--no-hooks` is the flag that disables them.
explanation: `--atomic` turns a failed deployment into a self-healing one: Helm waits for Deployments, StatefulSets, Services, PVCs and Jobs to be ready (with `--wait`), and if the timeout elapses it reverts to the last good revision. Without it a failed upgrade leaves the release in status `failed` with half-applied resources. Pair it with a sensible `--timeout` (default 5m0s) so CI does not hang.
example:
$ helm upgrade --install web ./web -n shop \
    --atomic --timeout 10m -f values-prod.yaml
# on failure: Error: UPGRADE FAILED ... rolling back to revision 4
diagram:
flowchart TD
    U["helm upgrade --atomic"] --> W["wait for readiness up to timeout"]
    W -->|"ready"| OK["release deployed"]
    W -->|"timeout or error"| RB["automatic rollback to previous revision"]
    RB --> F["command exits non-zero"]

prompt: A release is stuck with status `pending-upgrade` after a CI job was killed mid-upgrade, and every new `helm upgrade` fails with `another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress`. What is the recommended fix?
options: Roll back to the last deployed revision with `helm rollback <release> <revision>`
Run `helm uninstall` and reinstall from scratch
Delete the Deployment and let Helm recreate it
Run `helm repo update` to clear the lock
optionNotes: Correct. `helm rollback` to the last `deployed` revision (see `helm history`) replaces the pending state with a new, consistent revision; alternatively delete the pending revision's Secret.
Uninstalling destroys the workload and its history; it is a last resort, not the recommended fix for a stuck pending state.
The lock is the release Secret's status, not the workload; deleting the Deployment causes an outage and does not clear `pending-upgrade`.
`helm repo update` only refreshes local repository indexes and has nothing to do with release state.
explanation: Helm marks a release `pending-install`, `pending-upgrade`, or `pending-rollback` while an operation runs and refuses concurrent changes. If the client dies, that status never gets updated. `helm history` shows which revision is stuck; `helm rollback` to the last good revision writes a new revision and clears the block. Deleting the stuck `sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<n>` Secret is the manual equivalent.
example:
$ helm history web -n shop
REVISION  STATUS           DESCRIPTION
6         deployed         Upgrade complete
7         pending-upgrade  Preparing upgrade
$ helm rollback web 6 -n shop
Rollback was a success! Happy Helming!
diagram:
flowchart LR
    K["CI job killed mid-upgrade"] --> P["revision 7 pending-upgrade"]
    P --> E["new upgrade refused: operation in progress"]
    E -->|"helm rollback web 6"| R["revision 8 deployed"]
    R --> N["upgrades work again"]

prompt: In a chart template, what does `{{ include "web.labels" . | nindent 4 }}` do that `{{ template "web.labels" . }}` cannot?
options: `include` returns the named template's output as a string so it can be piped through functions like `nindent`
`include` renders the template from a subchart instead of the parent
`include` caches the result so the template is evaluated only once
`include` allows the named template to modify `.Values`
optionNotes: Correct. `template` is a Go template action that writes directly to the output and cannot be part of a pipeline; `include` is a Helm function that returns a string, so you can indent or transform it.
Both look up named templates by name across the whole rendering scope; neither is scoped specifically to subcharts.
There is no caching; the template is evaluated on every call.
Values are immutable in templates regardless of how a partial is called.
explanation: Named templates defined in `_helpers.tpl` with `define` are reused via `include`. Because `include` is a function returning a string, its output can be piped to `nindent` (newline plus indent), `quote`, `trim`, etc. The Helm docs recommend always preferring `include` over `template` for exactly this reason. The second argument (`.`) is the scope passed into the template.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    H["_helpers.tpl define web.labels"] -->|"include returns string"| P["pipeline nindent 4"]
    P --> M["metadata.labels in Deployment"]
    H -.->|"template writes directly, no pipeline"| X["cannot indent"]

prompt: Which template function makes rendering fail with a custom message when a value the chart cannot work without is missing?
options: `required`
`default`
`fail`
`empty`
optionNotes: Correct. `{{ required "msg" .Values.x }}` returns the value if set and aborts rendering with `msg` if it is empty or nil.
`default` supplies a fallback instead of failing, which is the opposite behaviour.
`fail` unconditionally aborts rendering with a message; it is useful inside an `if` but does not itself test a value. `required` is the purpose-built function.
`empty` returns a boolean and does not stop rendering by itself.
explanation: `required` is the idiomatic guard for values such as a database host or an image repository that have no sensible default. It produces a clear error at `helm install`, `helm template`, or `helm lint --strict` time instead of a broken manifest reaching the cluster. For richer validation, combine it with a `values.schema.json`.
example:
env:
  - name: DB_HOST
    value: {{ required "db.host must be set (use --set db.host=...)" .Values.db.host | quote }}

$ helm install web ./web
Error: execution error at (web/templates/deployment.yaml:23:22): db.host must be set (use --set db.host=...)
diagram:
flowchart TD
    V[".Values.db.host"] --> R{"required"}
    R -->|"set"| M["value rendered into manifest"]
    R -->|"empty or nil"| E["render aborts with custom message"]

prompt: A chart ships a Job annotated `helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade`. On `helm upgrade`, when does that Job run relative to the main manifests?
options: Before any of the release's regular manifests are applied for that upgrade, and the upgrade waits for it to complete
In parallel with the regular manifests
After the regular manifests are applied but before readiness is checked
Only on the first install; upgrades ignore `pre-upgrade`
optionNotes: Correct. Pre-upgrade hooks are loaded, applied, and waited on (Jobs must succeed) before Helm applies the rest of the chart; a failing hook aborts the upgrade.
Hooks are sequential relative to the main manifests; only hooks with the same weight may be applied together.
That describes `post-upgrade`, which runs after the manifests are applied.
`pre-upgrade` runs on every upgrade; `pre-install` is the hook that runs only on install.
explanation: Hooks let a chart run work at lifecycle points: `pre-install`, `post-install`, `pre-delete`, `post-delete`, `pre-upgrade`, `post-upgrade`, `pre-rollback`, `post-rollback`, and `test`. Hook resources are not tracked as part of the release, so by default they are left behind after they run; add `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy` (for example `before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded`) to clean them up. Database migrations are the classic `pre-upgrade` use case.
example:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-migrate
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade,pre-install
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
diagram:
flowchart LR
    U["helm upgrade"] --> PH["pre-upgrade hooks e.g. migrate Job"]
    PH -->|"Job succeeds"| M["apply regular manifests"]
    M --> PO["post-upgrade hooks"]
    PH -->|"Job fails"| X["upgrade aborted"]

prompt: Two `pre-install` hooks have `helm.sh/hook-weight` values of `"-5"` and `"10"`. In what order does Helm run them?
options: Weight `-5` first, then `10`; lower weights run first
Weight `10` first, then `-5`; higher weights run first
Both at the same time; weight only affects deletion order
Alphabetically by resource name; weight is ignored for `pre-install`
optionNotes: Correct. Hook weights are sorted ascending (negative numbers first); Helm applies each weight group and waits before moving to the next.
Higher weights run later, not earlier.
Weights define execution order for hooks; within the same weight Helm orders by kind and then name.
Weight is honoured for every hook type; name ordering is only the tiebreaker within the same weight.
explanation: `helm.sh/hook-weight` must be a quoted string containing an integer; the default is `0`. Helm sorts hooks of the same phase ascending by weight, then by kind, then by name, and applies them one group at a time. Use weights to guarantee, for example, that a ServiceAccount hook exists before the Job that uses it.
example:
annotations:
  "helm.sh/hook": pre-install
  "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"   # runs before weight 0 and 10
---
annotations:
  "helm.sh/hook": pre-install
  "helm.sh/hook-weight": "10"
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["hook weight -5 ServiceAccount"] --> B["hook weight 0 default"]
    B --> C["hook weight 10 Job"]
    C --> M["regular manifests applied"]

prompt: What is a library chart in Helm 3?
options: A chart with `type: library` in `Chart.yaml` that only provides named templates and cannot be installed on its own
A chart that packages a shared Docker image used by other charts
A chart stored in the `charts/` directory of another chart
A chart hosted in an OCI registry rather than an HTTP repository
optionNotes: Correct. Library charts expose reusable `define`d templates (usually in `_*.tpl` files) for other charts to `include`; `helm install` refuses to install them directly.
Helm charts never package container images; they reference them by repository and tag.
That describes a vendored subchart; a subchart can be an application chart or a library chart.
Where a chart is hosted is unrelated to its `type`.
explanation: `type` in `Chart.yaml` is either `application` (default, installable) or `library`. A library chart is declared as a dependency and pulled into `charts/`, after which its named templates become available to the parent. Files in a library chart's `templates/` that do not start with `_` are ignored, so it can never render Kubernetes objects itself. Organisations use library charts to standardise labels, probes, and security contexts across many application charts.
example:
# common/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: common
type: library
version: 0.3.0

# web/Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: common
    version: 0.3.0
    repository: oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts

# web/templates/deployment.yaml
{{- include "common.deployment" . }}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    L["library chart common type: library"] -->|"dependency"| W["web application chart"]
    L -->|"dependency"| A["api application chart"]
    W -->|"include common.deployment"| R["rendered Deployment"]
    L -.->|"helm install refused"| X["not installable alone"]

prompt: Which command pushes a packaged chart `web-1.4.0.tgz` to an OCI registry?
options: `helm push web-1.4.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts`
`helm repo push web-1.4.0.tgz ghcr.io/acme/charts`
`helm upload web-1.4.0.tgz --registry ghcr.io`
`docker push ghcr.io/acme/charts/web:1.4.0`
optionNotes: Correct. `helm push <tgz> oci://<registry>/<path>` uploads the chart as an OCI artifact; the chart name and version from `Chart.yaml` become the repository name and tag.
There is no `helm repo push`; `helm repo` manages HTTP repository entries only.
`helm upload` does not exist.
A chart is not a Docker image; although it is stored as an OCI artifact, only `helm push` produces the correct media types.
explanation: OCI support became GA in Helm 3.8. After `helm registry login ghcr.io`, `helm package` produces the `.tgz` and `helm push` stores it at `oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/web:1.4.0`. Consumers install with `helm install web oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/web --version 1.4.0` with no `helm repo add` step, and the same registry can hold the app's images. Note that OCI references use `oci://` and no `index.yaml` is involved.
example:
$ helm registry login ghcr.io -u $USER --password-stdin
$ helm package ./web            # web-1.4.0.tgz
$ helm push web-1.4.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts
Pushed: ghcr.io/acme/charts/web:1.4.0
$ helm install web oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/web --version 1.4.0
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["helm package ./web"] --> T["web-1.4.0.tgz"]
    T -->|"helm push oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts"| R["OCI registry web:1.4.0"]
    R -->|"helm install oci://..."| K["cluster"]
    R -->|"helm pull oci://..."| L["local tgz"]

prompt: In a parent chart's `values.yaml`, how do you override the `replicaCount` of a subchart named `redis`?
options: Nest it under the subchart name: `redis:\n  replicaCount: 3`
Use a dotted key: `redis.replicaCount: 3`
Put it under `global.redis.replicaCount`
Subchart values cannot be overridden by the parent; use `--set` at install time
optionNotes: Correct. A parent passes values to a subchart by placing them under a top-level key matching the subchart's name (or its `alias`); the subchart then sees them as its own `.Values`.
In YAML a dotted key is a literal string key, not a path; the subchart would not see it. Dotted paths are only for `--set`.
`global` values are visible to every chart as `.Values.global.*`; they do not map onto a subchart's own top-level keys.
Parents can override subchart values freely; that is the main way umbrella charts configure their components.
explanation: Values flow downward: the parent's `redis:` block is merged over the subchart's own `values.yaml` and exposed to it as `.Values`. A subchart cannot read its parent's values except through `global:`, which is copied into every chart. The same nesting applies on the command line: `--set redis.replicaCount=3`. If a dependency uses `alias`, the key must match the alias.
example:
# web/values.yaml
replicaCount: 2          # web's own value
redis:                   # forwarded to the redis subchart as .Values
  replicaCount: 3
  auth:
    enabled: false
global:
  imageRegistry: ghcr.io/acme   # visible to web AND redis
diagram:
flowchart TD
    P["parent values.yaml"] -->|"redis: block"| S["redis subchart .Values"]
    P -->|"global: block"| G["global copied to every chart"]
    G --> S
    G --> W["parent templates"]
    S -.->|"cannot read parent values"| P

prompt: `helm upgrade` fails with `Error: UPGRADE FAILED: rendered manifests contain a resource that already exists ... invalid ownership metadata; annotation validation error: missing key "meta.helm.sh/release-name"`. What does this mean and what is the standard fix?
options: The resource was created outside Helm; add the `meta.helm.sh/release-name` and `release-namespace` annotations plus the `app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm` label so Helm adopts it
The release Secret is corrupt; delete all `sh.helm.release.v1.*` Secrets and reinstall
The chart is missing `_helpers.tpl`; regenerate the chart with `helm create`
Two charts define the same named template; rename the `define` block
optionNotes: Correct. Since Helm 3.2 an existing object is adopted only if it carries the ownership annotations and managed-by label; adding them (with `kubectl annotate` and `kubectl label`) lets the upgrade take it over without deleting it.
The release history is fine; the conflict is between the rendered manifest and a pre-existing cluster object.
Helpers are unrelated; the message is about live resource ownership metadata.
Duplicate named templates do not produce an ownership error.
explanation: Helm refuses to overwrite objects it did not create, to avoid clobbering resources managed by another release or by `kubectl`. The fix is to annotate the object with `meta.helm.sh/release-name=<release>` and `meta.helm.sh/release-namespace=<ns>` and label it `app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=Helm`; Helm will then adopt it on the next upgrade. The alternative (`kubectl delete` then upgrade) causes downtime for that object.
example:
$ kubectl annotate svc web -n shop \
    meta.helm.sh/release-name=web meta.helm.sh/release-namespace=shop
$ kubectl label svc web -n shop app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=Helm
$ helm upgrade --install web ./web -n shop
diagram:
flowchart TD
    E["object exists without Helm ownership metadata"] --> F["upgrade refused: invalid ownership metadata"]
    F -->|"kubectl annotate release-name and release-namespace"| A["annotations added"]
    A -->|"kubectl label managed-by Helm"| L["label added"]
    L --> U["helm upgrade adopts the object"]

prompt: A template uses `{{ (lookup "v1" "Secret" .Release.Namespace "db-creds").data.password }}` to reuse an existing secret. It works with `helm install` but renders an empty value with `helm template`. Why?
options: `lookup` needs a live API connection; `helm template` runs offline so it returns an empty map
`helm template` cannot read Secrets for security reasons but can read ConfigMaps
The Secret must be in the `default` namespace for `helm template`
`lookup` only works inside hooks
optionNotes: Correct. `lookup` queries the cluster at render time; `helm template` and `--dry-run` (client mode) never contact the API server, so `lookup` returns an empty object and any field access yields nil.
There is no resource-type restriction; every kind is unreachable offline.
Namespace does not matter offline; the function simply has no cluster to query.
`lookup` works in any template, not just hooks.
explanation: `lookup` is powerful for idempotent secrets (generate once, then reuse) but makes charts non-deterministic and unusable in pure-render workflows such as GitOps or `helm template` piped to policy tools. Guard it with a default and, when you must inspect server data, use `helm install --dry-run=server` (Helm 3.13+), which performs lookups against the cluster.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    T["template calls lookup"] --> M{"render mode"}
    M -->|"helm install or --dry-run=server"| K["API server returns Secret"]
    M -->|"helm template or --dry-run=client"| E["empty map returned"]
    E --> N["field access yields nil"]

prompt: What is the purpose of the `--post-renderer` flag on `helm install`, `helm upgrade`, and `helm template`?
options: It pipes the fully rendered manifests through an external executable (such as Kustomize) so they can be modified before Helm applies them
It re-renders templates a second time to resolve `tpl` strings
It runs `helm test` automatically after the release is deployed
It renders hooks after the main manifests instead of before
optionNotes: Correct. The post-renderer receives the rendered YAML on stdin and must write modified YAML to stdout; Helm then tracks and applies the modified output as the release manifest.
`tpl` is evaluated during the normal render pass; there is no second pass.
Tests are run explicitly with `helm test`; post-renderers do not trigger them.
Hook ordering is controlled by hook annotations, not by post-rendering.
explanation: Post-rendering lets you patch third-party charts without forking them: inject sidecars, add labels, or set security contexts using Kustomize or a script. Because the modified output is what Helm stores in the release Secret, `helm get manifest` and rollbacks remain consistent. A common pattern is a small shell wrapper that runs `kustomize build` over the stdin manifests.
example:
$ cat kustomize.sh
#!/bin/sh
cat > all.yaml
kustomize build . && rm all.yaml

$ helm upgrade --install web bitnami/nginx \
    --post-renderer ./kustomize.sh --post-renderer-args=--enable-helm
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["chart and values"] -->|"render"| Y["rendered YAML"]
    Y -->|"stdin"| PR["post-renderer e.g. kustomize"]
    PR -->|"stdout"| M["modified manifests"]
    M --> K["applied and stored in release Secret"]

prompt: Which command lists the revisions of a release, showing each revision's status and chart version?
options: `helm history <release>`
`helm list --all`
`helm status <release>`
`helm get all <release>`
optionNotes: Correct. `helm history` prints every stored revision with its status (`deployed`, `superseded`, `failed`, `pending-*`), chart, app version, and description.
`helm list` shows releases (one line each) with the current revision only; `--all` adds failed and pending releases.
`helm status` reports the current revision's status, notes, and resources, not the full history.
`helm get all` dumps the hooks, manifest, notes, and values for one revision.
explanation: Every install, upgrade, or rollback writes a new revision Secret, and `helm history` reads them all. The revision numbers it shows are what you pass to `helm rollback` and `helm get values --revision`. By default Helm keeps the last 10 revisions (`--history-max`), so very old revisions are pruned.
example:
$ helm history web -n shop
REVISION  UPDATED                   STATUS      CHART      APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
1         Mon Sep  1 10:02:11 2026  superseded  web-1.3.0  2.8.0        Install complete
2         Tue Sep  2 09:15:40 2026  superseded  web-1.4.0  2.9.1        Upgrade complete
3         Thu Sep  4 16:48:03 2026  deployed    web-1.3.0  2.8.0        Rollback to 1
diagram:

    U --> R["rollback creates revision 3"]
    R -->|"helm history"| H["list of all revisions with status"]

prompt: A chart's `Chart.yaml` has `version: 1.4.0` and `appVersion: "2.9.1"`. You release a new build of the application with no changes to the templates or values. What should you bump?
options: Both: set `appVersion` to the new application version and increment the chart `version`, because a chart with the same version must not be republished with different content
Only `appVersion`; chart `version` only changes when templates change
Only `version`; `appVersion` is informational and should stay fixed
Neither; use `--set image.tag` at install time instead
optionNotes: Correct. Chart repositories and OCI registries treat a chart version as immutable, so any change to the packaged chart, including `appVersion`, requires a new chart `version` (a patch bump is typical).
Changing `appVersion` changes the package contents, so republishing `1.4.0` would break consumers who cached it and violates SemVer immutability.
`appVersion` is what `helm list` and `helm history` display and what many charts default the image tag from; leaving it stale is misleading.
Overriding at install time is valid for one-off deploys, but publishing a new app release should be captured in the chart.
explanation: `version` is the chart's own SemVer 2 version and is the immutable identifier in `index.yaml` or the OCI tag. `appVersion` is a free-form string describing the application and is often used as the default image tag via `.Chart.AppVersion`. Any change to the chart's content, including only `appVersion`, must ship as a new chart version. Tools like chart-releaser or `helm package --version --app-version` can set both in CI.
example:
$ helm package ./web --version 1.4.1 --app-version 2.10.0
# templates/deployment.yaml
image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["app release 2.10.0"] --> AV["appVersion 2.10.0"]
    AV --> CV["chart version 1.4.0 to 1.4.1"]
    CV --> P["immutable package web-1.4.1.tgz"]
    CV -.->|"republish 1.4.0"| X["breaks cached consumers"]

prompt: What is the role of `index.yaml` in a classic (HTTP) Helm chart repository?
options: It lists every chart and version in the repository with its download URL and digest, so `helm repo update` and `helm search repo` can work
It is the default values file applied to every chart in the repository
It stores login credentials for the repository
It is the `Chart.yaml` of the most recent chart
optionNotes: Correct. `index.yaml` is generated by `helm repo index` (or chart-releaser) and is the only file a client fetches during `helm repo update`; entries point at the `.tgz` packages.
Values are packaged inside each chart; the repository index has nothing to do with them.
Credentials are stored client-side in `repositories.yaml` or via `--username/--password`; the index is public metadata.
The index aggregates metadata from all charts, not just one.
explanation: A chart repository is just an HTTP server serving `index.yaml` plus chart tarballs. The index contains, per chart name, a list of versions with `urls`, `digest`, `created`, and the chart metadata. When you add a repository, Helm caches the index locally and resolves `helm install repo/chart --version` from it. OCI registries replace this model: there is no index, and versions are discovered from registry tags.
example:
$ helm repo index ./public --url https://charts.example.com
$ head public/index.yaml
apiVersion: v1
entries:
  web:
  - apiVersion: v2
    version: 1.4.1
    appVersion: 2.10.0
    urls:
    - https://charts.example.com/web-1.4.1.tgz
    digest: sha256:...
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["web-1.4.1.tgz packages"] -->|"helm repo index"| I["index.yaml"]
    I -->|"helm repo update"| C["client cache"]
    C -->|"helm search repo web"| S["versions listed"]
    C -->|"helm install acme/web"| D["downloads tgz by url"]

prompt: `helm install` fails with `Error: values don't meet the specifications of the schema(s) in the following chart(s): web: - image.tag: Invalid type. Expected: string, given: number` after you passed `--set image.tag=2024`. What is the cause and fix?
options: `--set` parses `2024` as an integer and the chart's `values.schema.json` requires a string; use `--set-string image.tag=2024` or quote it in a values file
The chart's `values.yaml` is malformed; run `helm lint` and fix the YAML
The Kubernetes version does not support numeric tags; upgrade the cluster
The schema file must be deleted because Helm 3 does not support JSON Schema
optionNotes: Correct. `--set` applies type inference (numbers, `true/false`, `null`), so `2024` becomes an int and fails a `"type": "string"` constraint; `--set-string` forces string typing.
The error comes from schema validation of the supplied values, not from `values.yaml` syntax.
Kubernetes never sees the values; Helm rejects them before rendering.
Helm 3 has supported `values.schema.json` since 3.0; removing it drops a useful safeguard.
explanation: `values.schema.json` in the chart root is a JSON Schema that Helm validates values against on `install`, `upgrade`, `lint`, and `template`. Its type checks interact with `--set`'s automatic typing: image tags like `2024` or `1.10` are especially prone to this. `--set-string` keeps the literal string, and `--set-json` lets you pass typed JSON explicitly. Values in a `-f` file follow normal YAML typing, so quote them there.
example:
$ helm install web ./web --set-string image.tag=2024
# or in values file
image:
  tag: "2024"

# values.schema.json excerpt
{"properties": {"image": {"properties": {"tag": {"type": "string"}}}}}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    S["--set image.tag=2024"] -->|"type inference"| N["integer 2024"]
    N --> V{"values.schema.json type string"}
    V -->|"fail"| E["install rejected"]
    SS["--set-string image.tag=2024"] --> STR["string 2024"]
    STR --> V
    V -->|"pass"| OK["render continues"]

prompt: Which of the following are built-in top-level objects available inside Helm templates? (Select all that apply.)
options: `.Release`
`.Values`
`.Chart`
`.Capabilities`
`.Cluster`
`.Env`
optionNotes: `.Release` exposes `Name`, `Namespace`, `Revision`, `IsInstall`, `IsUpgrade`, and `Service`; it is built in.
`.Values` is the merged result of `values.yaml`, `-f` files and `--set`; it is built in.
`.Chart` is the parsed `Chart.yaml` (`.Chart.Name`, `.Chart.Version`, `.Chart.AppVersion`); it is built in.
`.Capabilities` exposes `KubeVersion` and `APIVersions.Has` so templates can adapt to the target cluster; it is built in.
There is no `.Cluster` object; cluster information comes from `.Capabilities`.
Helm deliberately does not expose environment variables to templates; there is no `.Env`.
explanation: Helm passes a fixed set of objects into templates: `.Release`, `.Values`, `.Chart`, `.Files`, `.Capabilities`, `.Template`, and `.Subcharts`. Anything else must come through values. Note that `.Chart` fields are capitalised (`.Chart.Name`, not `.Chart.name`) because they map to Go struct fields, whereas `.Values` keys keep whatever casing the YAML used.
diagram:
flowchart TD
    T["template scope dot"] --> R[".Release name namespace revision"]
    T --> V[".Values merged config"]
    T --> C[".Chart metadata"]
    T --> K[".Capabilities KubeVersion APIVersions"]
    T --> F[".Files and .Template"]

prompt: Which statements about Helm chart hooks are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Hook resources are not tracked as part of the release and are not removed by `helm uninstall` unless a delete policy removes them
`helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation` deletes the previous hook resource before a new one is launched
A hook Job that fails causes the install or upgrade to fail
Hooks run with `--no-hooks` but their output is discarded
A resource can declare multiple hook phases in one annotation, such as `pre-install,pre-upgrade`
optionNotes: True. Hooks are applied but not stored in the release manifest, so `helm uninstall` ignores them; use delete policies or `pre-delete`/`post-delete` cleanup.
True. `before-hook-creation` is the default policy in Helm 3 and avoids `AlreadyExists` errors on the next run.
True. Helm waits for hook Jobs and Pods to complete; a failure aborts the operation (and triggers rollback with `--atomic`).
False. `--no-hooks` skips hooks entirely; they do not run at all.
True. A comma-separated list lets the same Job serve several lifecycle points.
explanation: Hooks are ordinary Kubernetes manifests with a `helm.sh/hook` annotation. Helm applies them at the right phase and blocks on Jobs and Pods, but because they are outside the release's tracked manifest, their lifecycle is governed only by `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy` (`before-hook-creation`, `hook-succeeded`, `hook-failed`). `--no-hooks` is useful for emergency upgrades when a migration hook is known to be broken.
example:
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-install,pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "1"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded

$ helm upgrade web ./web --no-hooks   # skip the migration Job this time
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["hook Job applied at phase"] --> W["Helm waits for completion"]
    W -->|"succeeded"| D["delete if hook-succeeded policy"]
    W -->|"failed"| F["operation fails"]
    N["next run"] -->|"before-hook-creation"| C["old hook deleted first"]

prompt: Which of the following are legitimate reasons `helm upgrade` might report no diff yet the running Pods are not updated? (Select all that apply.)
options: The image tag is unchanged (for example `latest`), so the Deployment spec is identical and Kubernetes does not roll Pods
A ConfigMap changed but the Deployment has no checksum annotation referencing it
The `values.yaml` change only affected a `NOTES.txt` template
Helm applied the manifest with `kubectl replace`, which never triggers rollouts
The release Secret exceeded 1 MiB and the manifest was truncated
optionNotes: True. Helm and Kubernetes compare specs; a mutable tag such as `latest` yields an identical Deployment, so no rollout occurs. Use immutable tags or `imagePullPolicy` plus a restart.
True. Pods do not restart when a mounted ConfigMap changes; the standard trick is a `checksum/config` annotation on the Pod template built with `sha256sum`.
True. `NOTES.txt` is rendered but not applied to the cluster, so changing it produces a new revision with no workload change.
False. Helm uses a three-way strategic merge patch; a spec change is still a spec change and triggers a rollout.
False. Helm errors out if the release Secret is too large rather than silently truncating.
explanation: A Helm upgrade only causes a rollout if the Pod template in the applied Deployment actually changes. Mutable image tags and ConfigMap edits are the two classic cases where the manifest looks the same to Kubernetes. The `checksum/config` annotation pattern forces a rollout whenever the ConfigMap template output changes; `helm diff` (plugin) shows exactly which fields differ before you upgrade.
example:
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
diagram:
flowchart TD
    U["helm upgrade"] --> P{"Pod template changed?"}
    P -->|"yes"| R["rollout new Pods"]
    P -->|"no: same tag or only ConfigMap"| S["Pods untouched"]
    CM["checksum/config annotation"] -->|"ConfigMap change alters template"| P

prompt: Which of these are valid ways to supply values to `helm install`? (Select all that apply.)
options: `-f values-prod.yaml` (repeatable; later files override earlier ones)
`--set key=value` and `--set-string key=value`
`--set-file key=path/to/file`
`--set-json 'key={"a":1}'`
`--values-env KEY=VALUE`
optionNotes: True. `-f`/`--values` can be given multiple times; the rightmost file wins on conflicting keys.
True. `--set` infers types; `--set-string` forces strings. Both override values files.
True. `--set-file` reads the file contents into the value, handy for certificates or large scripts.
True. `--set-json` (Helm 3.10+) accepts typed JSON, including nested objects and arrays.
False. There is no `--values-env`; environment variables must be substituted by your shell or CI before invoking Helm.
explanation: Helm merges values in this order, with later sources winning: chart `values.yaml`, parent overrides, `-f` files left to right, then the `--set*` family. Keep environment configuration in versioned values files and reserve `--set` for CI-provided values such as the image tag. Remember that `--set` uses `.` for nesting, `[i]` for list indexes and `\,` to escape commas.
example:
$ helm install web ./web \
    -f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml \
    --set-string image.tag=$GIT_SHA \
    --set-file tls.cert=./tls.crt \
    --set-json 'ingress.hosts=["a.example.com","b.example.com"]'
diagram:
flowchart LR
    D["chart values.yaml"] --> M["merge lowest to highest"]
    F["-f files left to right"] --> M
    S["--set --set-string --set-file --set-json"] --> M
    M --> R["final .Values"]

prompt: Which statements about `helm test` are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Test resources are Pods or Jobs annotated with `helm.sh/hook: test`
A test passes if its Pod exits with code 0
`helm test <release>` runs against an installed release, not a chart directory
Tests run automatically at the end of every `helm install`
`--logs` prints the test Pod logs after the run
optionNotes: True. In Helm 3 the test annotation is `helm.sh/hook: test` (the older `test-success` alias still works).
True. Helm waits for the Pod to complete; exit 0 is success, anything else marks the test failed.
True. Tests exercise a live release; you name the release, and Helm applies the test hooks in that namespace.
False. Tests only run when you invoke `helm test` explicitly (CI pipelines typically call it right after an install).
True. `--logs` streams each test Pod's logs, which is invaluable when a test fails in CI.
explanation: Chart tests live under `templates/tests/` and are ordinary Pods with the `test` hook annotation, for example a `wget` against the Service. They are a lightweight smoke test that the release is reachable. Because they are hooks, they are not part of the release manifest; add `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy` if you want them cleaned up.
example:
# templates/tests/test-connection.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: "{{ .Release.Name }}-test-connection"
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": test
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: wget
      image: busybox
      command: ['wget', '{{ .Release.Name }}-web:80']

$ helm test web -n shop --logs
diagram:
flowchart LR
    I["helm install web"] --> T["helm test web --logs"]
    T --> P["test Pod from templates/tests"]
    P -->|"exit 0"| OK["TEST SUITE passed"]
    P -->|"non-zero"| F["failed with logs"]

prompt: An umbrella chart declares subcharts `api`, `worker`, and `redis`. Which techniques correctly control which subcharts are rendered and how they are configured? (Select all that apply.)
options: Add `condition: redis.enabled` to the dependency entry and set `redis.enabled: false` in values to skip it
Use `tags:` on dependencies plus a top-level `tags:` map in values to toggle groups of subcharts
Use `alias:` to install the same subchart twice under different names, each with its own values block
Put shared settings under `global:` so every subchart can read them via `.Values.global`
Set `enabled: false` inside the subchart's own `Chart.yaml`
optionNotes: True. `condition` names a boolean path in the parent's values; when false the subchart is skipped entirely.
True. Tags provide group toggles; a `condition` on the same dependency takes precedence over tags.
True. `alias` lets you declare `redis` twice as `cache` and `queue`, each configured under its alias key.
True. `global` is the sanctioned way to share values downward across all subcharts.
False. `Chart.yaml` has no `enabled` field; enabling is controlled from the parent's `Chart.yaml` dependencies and values.
explanation: Umbrella charts compose applications from subcharts vendored into `charts/` by `helm dependency update`. Each `dependencies[]` entry supports `condition`, `tags`, `alias`, and `import-values`. Conditions are evaluated from the parent's values, so `--set redis.enabled=false` works from the command line. Keep umbrella charts thin: their job is wiring and shared `global` values, not application logic.
example:
# platform/Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: redis
    version: 19.x.x
    repository: oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts
    condition: redis.enabled
    tags: [backend]
  - name: redis
    alias: queue
    version: 19.x.x
    repository: oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts
    condition: queue.enabled
diagram:
flowchart TD
    U["umbrella chart"] --> A["api subchart"]
    U --> W["worker subchart"]
    U -->|"condition redis.enabled"| R["redis subchart"]
    U -->|"alias queue"| Q["redis as queue"]
    G["global values"] --> A
    G --> W
    G --> R

prompt: Helm 3 requires a server-side component (Tiller) running in the cluster to manage releases.
explanation: Tiller was removed in Helm 3. The `helm` CLI talks directly to the Kubernetes API using your kubeconfig credentials, and release state is stored as Secrets in the release namespace. This removed the major security concern of Helm 2, where Tiller often ran with cluster-admin.
example:
$ helm version --short
v3.19.0+g...
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep tiller   # nothing: no Tiller in Helm 3
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["helm CLI with kubeconfig"] -->|"direct API calls"| K["Kubernetes API server"]
    K --> S["release Secrets in namespace"]
    T["Tiller Helm 2 only"] -.->|"removed"| K

prompt: `helm rollback web 2` restores revision 2 in place, so afterwards `helm history` still shows revision 2 as the latest entry.
explanation: A rollback never rewrites history. Helm takes the chart and values from revision 2 and writes a brand-new revision (for example revision 4) with description `Rollback to 2`. This keeps the audit trail intact and means you can roll back a rollback. Running `helm rollback web` with no revision number targets the previous revision.
example:
$ helm rollback web 2 -n shop
$ helm history web -n shop
REVISION  STATUS      DESCRIPTION
2         superseded  Upgrade complete
3         superseded  Upgrade complete
4         deployed    Rollback to 2
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R2["revision 2 deployed"] --> R3["revision 3 bad upgrade"]
    R3 -->|"helm rollback web 2"| R4["revision 4 = contents of 2"]
    R4 --> H["history keeps 2 3 4"]

prompt: In a Helm 3 `Chart.yaml`, the `version` field must be a valid Semantic Versioning 2.0 string, but `appVersion` can be any string.
explanation: Helm parses `version` with a SemVer library and uses it for `--version` constraints (`~1.4.0`, `>=1.0.0 <2.0.0`) and repository index ordering, so it must be valid SemVer 2. `appVersion` is purely informational (displayed by `helm list` and usable via `.Chart.AppVersion`) and may be something like `"2.9.1"`, `"v2.9"`, or a git SHA. Quote it in YAML to prevent `1.10` being parsed as the float `1.1`.
example:
apiVersion: v2
name: web
version: 1.4.0-rc.1       # valid SemVer 2 prerelease
appVersion: "2026.09-a1b2c3d"  # any string, quoted
diagram:
flowchart LR
    V["version 1.4.0"] -->|"SemVer 2 required"| C["constraints and index ordering"]
    A["appVersion any string"] -->|"informational"| L["helm list and .Chart.AppVersion"]

prompt: The `tpl` function lets a chart render a string from values as if it were a template, so a user can write `{{ .Release.Name }}` inside `values.yaml` and have it expanded.
explanation: `tpl` takes a string and the current scope and evaluates the string as a Go template. This is how charts allow values like `hostname: "{{ .Release.Name }}.{{ .Values.domain }}"` or template snippets in ConfigMap data. Because `tpl` re-parses at render time it is slower than a normal template and errors surface with less helpful positions, so use it only where user-provided templating is genuinely needed.
example:
# values.yaml
ingress:
  host: "{{ .Release.Name }}.apps.example.com"

# templates/ingress.yaml
- host: {{ tpl .Values.ingress.host . | quote }}
# renders: web.apps.example.com for release web
diagram:
flowchart LR
    V["values string with template syntax"] -->|"tpl string dot"| E["evaluated as Go template"]
    E --> O["expanded string in manifest"]
    V -.->|"without tpl"| L["literal braces emitted"]

prompt: Which `helm` subcommand checks a chart directory for structural problems and template errors without installing it?
explanation: `helm lint` validates `Chart.yaml`, renders templates with default (or `-f`) values, and reports errors and warnings such as missing icons, unquoted `appVersion`, or unparseable YAML. `--strict` turns warnings into failures. It is a cheap first gate in a chart CI pipeline, usually followed by `helm template` plus a Kubernetes schema check.
example:
$ helm lint ./web --strict -f values-prod.yaml
==> Linting ./web
[INFO] Chart.yaml: icon is recommended
1 chart(s) linted, 0 chart(s) failed
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["chart directory"] -->|"helm lint --strict"| L["Chart.yaml and template checks"]
    L -->|"ok"| T["helm template"]
    T --> K["kubeconform or kubectl dry-run"]
    L -->|"errors"| F["CI fails"]

prompt: Which `helm` subcommand bundles a chart directory into a versioned `.tgz` archive ready to be pushed or served from a repository?
explanation: `helm package ./web` produces `web-<version>.tgz` named from `Chart.yaml`. Flags such as `--version`, `--app-version`, `--dependency-update` (`-u`) and `--sign` (provenance file) are commonly used in CI. The resulting archive is what `helm push` uploads to an OCI registry or `helm repo index` catalogs in an HTTP repository.
example:
$ helm package ./web -u --version 1.4.1 --app-version 2.10.0
Successfully packaged chart and saved it to: /work/web-1.4.1.tgz
diagram:
flowchart LR
    D["web/ directory"] -->|"helm package"| T["web-1.4.1.tgz"]
    T -->|"helm push"| O["OCI registry"]
    T -->|"helm repo index"| R["HTTP repo index.yaml"]

prompt: What is the exact file name of the JSON Schema file placed in a chart's root directory that Helm uses to validate supplied values?
explanation: Helm looks for `values.schema.json` next to `values.yaml`. If present, the merged values are validated against it during `helm install`, `helm upgrade`, `helm lint`, and `helm template`, and a violation aborts the operation with a readable error. Schemas can enforce required keys, types, enums and patterns, giving chart users faster feedback than a template-time `required` call.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    V["merged values"] --> S{"values.schema.json"}
    S -->|"valid"| R["templates rendered"]
    S -->|"invalid"| E["install aborted with schema error"]

prompt: Which `helm upgrade` flag makes Helm create the release if it does not already exist, so one command works for both first deploy and later updates?
explanation: `helm upgrade --install` (short `-i`) is the idempotent form used in almost every CI pipeline. If the release is absent it behaves like `helm install`; otherwise it performs an upgrade. Combine it with `--create-namespace`, `--atomic`, and a values file for a fully reproducible deploy step.
example:
$ helm upgrade --install web ./web -n shop --create-namespace \
    -f values-prod.yaml --atomic --timeout 10m
diagram:
flowchart TD
    U["helm upgrade --install web"] --> E{"release exists?"}
    E -->|"no"| I["install revision 1"]
    E -->|"yes"| G["upgrade to next revision"]

prompt: Which `helm dependency` subcommand resolves the entries in `Chart.yaml`, downloads the subcharts into `charts/`, and writes `Chart.lock`?
explanation: `helm dependency update` reads `dependencies:` from `Chart.yaml`, resolves each version constraint against the repository or OCI registry, downloads the tarballs into `charts/`, and pins the exact versions in `Chart.lock`. `helm dependency build` instead reproduces `charts/` from an existing `Chart.lock`, which is what you want in CI for repeatable builds. `helm dependency list` shows the current status of each dependency.
example:
$ helm dependency update ./platform
Saving 2 charts
Downloading redis from repo oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts
Deleting outdated charts
$ ls platform/charts
redis-19.6.2.tgz
$ helm dependency build ./platform   # CI: rebuild from Chart.lock
diagram:
flowchart LR
    Y["Chart.yaml dependencies"] -->|"helm dependency update"| C["charts/ tgz files"]
    Y -->|"helm dependency update"| L["Chart.lock pinned"]
    L -->|"helm dependency build"| C

prompt: Which template function converts a values structure (map or list) into properly formatted YAML so a whole block such as `resources` or `nodeSelector` can be passed through to a manifest?
explanation: `toYaml` serialises any value to YAML text. Combined with `nindent`, it is the standard way to let users supply arbitrary Kubernetes structures (resources, affinity, tolerations, extra env) without the chart having to model every field. The related `toJson`, `fromYaml`, and `fromJson` functions handle the other directions.
example:
# values.yaml
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi

# templates/deployment.yaml
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    V[".Values.resources map"] -->|"toYaml"| Y["YAML text"]
    Y -->|"nindent 12"| M["embedded in Deployment container spec"]

prompt: What is the name of the widely used Helm plugin that shows a colourised preview of what `helm upgrade` would change in the cluster before you run it?
explanation: The `helm diff` plugin (databus23/helm-diff) renders the proposed release and compares it with the manifest stored in the current revision, printing a unified diff. `helm diff upgrade web ./web -f values-prod.yaml` is a common CI gate, and `helm diff rollback` and `helm diff revision` compare stored revisions. Since Helm 3.13, `helm upgrade --dry-run=server` can complement it by validating against the API server, but it does not show a diff.
example:
$ helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff
$ helm diff upgrade web ./web -n shop -f values-prod.yaml
shop, web, Deployment (apps) has changed:
-          image: ghcr.io/acme/web:2.9.1
+          image: ghcr.io/acme/web:2.10.0
diagram:
flowchart LR
    N["new chart and values"] -->|"render"| P["proposed manifest"]
    S["current release manifest from Secret"] --> D["helm diff upgrade"]
    P --> D
    D --> O["unified diff shown before upgrade"]

prompt: Which `helm` subcommand removes a release and all the Kubernetes resources it manages from the cluster?
explanation: `helm uninstall <release>` deletes every resource in the release manifest and, by default, the release history Secrets as well. Use `--keep-history` to retain the revisions so `helm rollback` can resurrect the release later. Hook resources and CRDs installed from the `crds/` directory are not removed. `helm delete` remains as an alias from Helm 2 days.
example:
$ helm uninstall web -n shop --keep-history
release "web" uninstalled
$ helm history web -n shop
REVISION  STATUS       DESCRIPTION
3         uninstalled  Uninstallation complete
diagram:
flowchart LR
    U["helm uninstall web"] --> R["delete tracked resources"]
    U -->|"default"| S["delete release Secrets"]
    U -->|"--keep-history"| K["Secrets retained for rollback"]
    U -.->|"not removed"| C["CRDs from crds/ and hook resources"]

prompt: Which `helm` subcommand downloads a chart from a repository or OCI registry to the local filesystem without installing it (add `--untar` to expand it)?
explanation: `helm pull` retrieves the packaged chart so you can inspect it, vendor it into a Git repository, or audit its templates before deploying. It works with both `repo/chart` references and `oci://` URLs, supports `--version`, and `--untar` extracts the archive into a directory. `helm show values` is the lighter alternative when you only need the default values.
example:
$ helm pull oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/web --version 1.4.1 --untar
$ ls web
Chart.yaml  values.yaml  templates  charts
$ helm show values oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/web --version 1.4.1
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["OCI registry or HTTP repo"] -->|"helm pull --untar"| L["local chart directory"]
    L --> I["inspect templates and values"]
    L --> G["vendor into Git for GitOps"]

prompt: Which `helm upgrade` flag tells Helm to start from the values of the previous revision and merge the new `--set`/`-f` values on top, instead of resetting to the chart's defaults?
explanation: `--reuse-values` carries forward the last revision's computed values, which is convenient for quick `--set` tweaks but dangerous across chart version bumps because new defaults in the updated `values.yaml` are ignored. Helm 3.14 added `--reset-then-reuse-values`, which takes the new chart's defaults and then re-applies the previous overrides, a safer middle ground. The recommended practice remains passing the full values file on every upgrade.
example:
$ helm upgrade web ./web --reuse-values --set replicas=5
# keeps image.tag from the last revision, but ignores new defaults in values.yaml
$ helm upgrade web ./web --reset-then-reuse-values   # Helm 3.14+
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["previous revision values"] -->|"--reuse-values"| M["merge"]
    N["new --set and -f"] --> M
    M --> R["values for new revision"]
    D["new chart defaults"] -.->|"ignored with --reuse-values"| M
